html:
The preceding subsections covered (i) the objectives the cortex implicitly minimizes—both overarching intrinsic goals and their neuron-/synapse-local decompositions—and (ii) the mechanisms by which error-like signals are computed, represented, precision-weighted, and routed through cortical circuitry. The remaining question is the one that turns an abstract optimization story into a physical one: given these error signals, what cortex-specific plasticity rules actually implement the update step? In other words, how does neocortex convert moment-to-moment mismatches into lasting changes in synaptic efficacy, intrinsic excitability, and circuit wiring, while remaining stable, metabolically viable, and continuously online?

At the foundation are the synaptic and structural plasticity primitives already developed in "The Fundamentals." Here we will not re-derive those mechanisms in detail, but we will explicitly build on them. In cortex, Hebbian rules and spike timing-dependent plasticity (STDP) supply the canonical local substrate for credit assignment: synapses are biased to strengthen when presynaptic activity reliably contributes to postsynaptic depolarization (and to weaken when it does not), with millisecond-scale spike timing (or more generally, local voltage trajectories) shaping the sign and magnitude of change. These two-factor rules, however, are only the entry point. The cortex rarely learns from a single, clean teaching channel; instead, it learns under a superposition of constraints and teaching pressures that must be integrated without destabilizing the network.

The key bridge from error signals to weight change is that cortical neurons are simultaneously subject to multiple concurrent "error" terms. Some are explicitly instructive in a dendritic-computation sense: apical-basal voltage mismatches can encode a local disagreement between top-down feedback and bottom-up drive, providing a compartment-specific teaching signal for synapses that contributed to the mismatch. Others are predictive and temporal: self-predictive errors track whether a neuron or microcircuit correctly anticipated its own near-future activity, enabling learning rules that are locally self-supervised. Still others enforce viability constraints: homeostatic rate errors penalize sustained deviations from target activity regimes; metabolic cost gradients favor sparse, low-energy solutions; and neuromodulatory reinforcement-learning (RL) signals provide low-bandwidth, state- and outcome-dependent teaching that gates when locally eligible synapses are actually modified. In cortex, these heterogeneous pressures do not remain separate all the way down to the synapse. They converge on a shared biophysical currency: dendritic voltage and Ca2+^{2+} dynamics with a strongly compartment-specific spatiotemporal structure 1, 2, 3. The "meaning" of an error signal, in practice, is therefore expressed as a deformation of the neuron’s dendritic voltage landscape, and as a corresponding pattern of Ca2+^{2+} influx and buffering across spines, branches, and apical tufts.

The job of this section, then, is to track the transduction chain: error signals →\rightarrow voltage/Ca2+^{2+} landscape →\rightarrow synaptic and structural change. Concretely, we will focus on the cortical implementation details that determine which plasticity rules dominate where and when. The underlying synaptic and structural mechanisms remain those reviewed in “The Fundamentals”; the emphasis here is on why cortex, given its dendritic geometry, laminar wiring, and modulatory meta-control, instantiates them in a way that looks like a unified optimizer despite being implemented as many local, partially gated learning rules operating in parallel. A 2026 model illustrates calcium-mediated interactions between neighboring spines (Figure). The study compares predicted responses to stimulation protocols (Figure).
